title: How to Get Unhigh: Ways to Come Down Comfortably
h1: Too High? Practical Ways to Come Down from Cannabis
metaDescription: How to get unhigh: what being too high feels like, how long it lasts by format, calm steps that help, which remedies have evidence and when to get help.
excerpt: Too much THC feels awful, but it passes. Here's how long it usually lasts, what genuinely helps, what the evidence says about home remedies and when to call for help.
keyTakeaways: Feeling too high is miserable but temporary, and time is the only sure way down.
Smoked or vaped cannabis usually tapers off within 2 to 3 hours; edibles can last 4 to 12 hours.
Water, a quiet room and slow breathing make the wait easier. Skip alcohol and don't drive.
Call 911 for chest pain, fainting or trouble breathing, and Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 if a child eats cannabis.
body:
If you've had more THC than you meant to, start here: the feeling passes. Learning how to get unhigh mostly means helping the time go by safely. Stop using, find a calm spot, sip some water and let your body clear it. Here's how to come down from a high, how long it usually takes and when to get help.

## Signs you're too high, and what a cannabis hangover feels like

The CDC describes the signs of using too much cannabis as the usual effects, only stronger:

- Extreme confusion
- Anxiety, paranoia or panic
- A fast heart rate or higher blood pressure
- Delusions or hallucinations
- Severe nausea or vomiting

The CDC also says a fatal overdose from cannabis alone is unlikely. That doesn't make it harmless.

A heavy night can show up the next morning too, especially after a late edible. Some people wake up still feeling a little foggy or slow, often called a cannabis hangover. Take a slow start with water and breakfast, and don't drive until you feel fully clear.

## Why THC can tip into too much

THC acts on cannabinoid receptors in the brain. At a comfortable dose, that can feel pleasant. Past your comfort zone, the same effects can turn into anxiety or distrust. NIDA notes these reactions are more common with large amounts, strong products and less experience, and that THC can raise heart rate right after use.

Edibles add a timing trap. Because they're slow to start, people often reach for more before the first dose lands. Our look at [why cannabis sometimes hits harder than expected](/blog/why-cannabis-can-feel-stronger/) covers other surprises.

## How to get unhigh: what actually helps

If you're too high, what to do first is simple: stop and settle in. Nothing switches THC off, but you can make the wait easier.

1. **Stop using,** and put the rest away.
2. **Move somewhere calm.** A familiar room, low light and a favorite show or playlist help the minutes pass.
3. **Slow your breathing.** Breathe in for a count of four and out for six. Many people find long exhales settling.
4. **Sip water.** Dry mouth is common, as our guide to [cottonmouth and hydration](/blog/does-weed-dehydrate-you/) explains.
5. **Eat something light,** like toast or fruit, if you feel up to it.
6. **Rest.** Lie down if you feel dizzy, and let sleep come if it wants to.
7. **Shower only if you're steady.** Skip it if you feel faint or wobbly.

## Why to skip alcohol while you're high

A drink to take the edge off can backfire. The CDC says using alcohol and cannabis together is likely to cause more impairment than either one alone, and more impairment means more risk of getting hurt. Stick with water until you feel like yourself.

## How long coming down takes, by format

How long does a high last? It depends on how THC entered your body, plus your dose and tolerance. A widely cited review of cannabinoid research gives these typical windows:

| Format | Effects start | Strongest | How long it lasts |
|---|---|---|---|
| Smoked or vaped | Seconds to a few minutes | 15 to 30 minutes | Tapers off within 2 to 3 hours |
| Edibles and drinks | 30 to 90 minutes | 2 to 3 hours | About 4 to 12 hours |

Dabs follow the inhaled timeline, but NIDA notes they deliver a lot of THC very quickly. With edibles, the CDC says you may not feel anything for up to 2 hours, which is why people take a second dose too soon. Our [THC dosage guide](/blog/thc-dosage-guide/) covers timing in detail.

## Remedies people try, and what the evidence says

- **CBD.** Taking CBD to counteract THC sounds logical, but results are mixed. In a 2023 trial of 46 adults, adding CBD at common ratios did not reduce THC's effects on memory or psychotic-like symptoms.
- **Black pepper.** Using black pepper for a high rests on beta-caryophyllene, a terpene in pepper studied in the lab, as our [caryophyllene guide](/blog/caryophyllene-terpene/) explains. No human study has tested pepper for this.
- **Citrus peel.** Peel contains limonene, the terpene with the most promising early evidence here. In a small 2024 study of 20 adults, anxiety ratings tended to fall as more vaporized limonene was added to THC. The only clear drop in anxiety and paranoia came at the highest limonene dose, which 12 of them tried. Sniffing a lemon peel is not the same dose.
- **Pine nuts.** The idea points to pinene, a terpene named for pine trees. No research shows pine nuts change a high.
- **Ginger tea.** No study links ginger to a shorter high, though a warm mug can be calming to hold.

None of these lowers the THC in your body. Time does that.

## A short walk or staying put?

If you feel steady and a sober friend is with you, a slow walk somewhere familiar can be a welcome change of scene. Stay put if you feel dizzy or unsure of your footing. Either way, don't drive, bike or swim until the effects are fully gone.

## Prevention: dose, timing and setting

- **Dose:** Start low with any new product, and check the THC per serving or the percentage on the label.
- **Timing:** Give an edible a full 2 hours before taking more, and give inhaled cannabis 15 to 30 minutes to peak. Our list of [common edible myths](/blog/myths-about-edibles/) explains why waiting matters.
- **Setting:** Pick a familiar place, people you trust and an evening with nowhere to drive.
- **Tolerance:** After a break, your usual amount may feel stronger than you expect.
- **Questions:** Our budtenders are happy to talk through lower-dose options at any of our [Michigan stores](/dispensary-locations/).

## When to get medical help

- **Call 911** for chest pain, fainting, trouble breathing, a seizure, or someone who can't stay awake.
- **Call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222** if a child eats cannabis, even if they seem fine. The CDC notes that young children who swallow cannabis are more likely than older kids to need a hospital stay.
- **Get medical care** for vomiting that won't stop. After long-term, heavy use, it can point to cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome, which NIDA says often needs medical attention.
- **Get help** for hallucinations or panic that isn't easing.

If a pet gets into cannabis, call your veterinarian.

faq.q: How long does it take to stop being high?
faq.a: It depends on the format. Smoked or vaped cannabis usually peaks within 15 to 30 minutes and tapers off within 2 to 3 hours. Edibles can take 30 to 90 minutes to start and last about 4 to 12 hours. A bigger dose or a lower tolerance stretches those windows.

Not reliably. A 2019 review found CBD softened some of THC's effects in some studies but not others. A 2023 randomized trial found that CBD at common ratios didn't reduce THC's effects on memory or psychotic-like symptoms. CBD doesn't cause a high, but it isn't a dependable fix for one.

There's no good evidence that it does. The idea comes from beta-caryophyllene, a terpene in black pepper that has been studied in the lab, not in people coming down from a high. If you try it, sniff a few whole peppercorns rather than ground pepper.

You can take too much, though the CDC says a fatal overdose from cannabis alone is unlikely. Too much can still mean panic, a racing heart, vomiting or confusion, and children who eat cannabis can become seriously ill. If you're worried, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222.

faq.q: Should I go to the ER if I'm too high?
faq.a: Go, or call 911, if you have chest pain, faint, struggle to breathe, have a seizure or can't stop vomiting. For less urgent worries, Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 offers free expert advice around the clock. When in doubt, it's always fine to call.

review.summary: 34 claims checked: 28 ok, 6 fixed (0 wrong, 2 unsupported, 4 overstated); 1 ok claim also got a precision edit.

claims.claim: CDC: signs of too much cannabis are the usual effects but more severe: extreme confusion; anxiety, paranoia or panic; fast heart rate or higher blood pressure; delusions or hallucinations; severe nausea or vomiting
claims.source: https://www.cdc.gov/cannabis/faq/index.html (WebFetch + curl 2026-10-24): "The signs of using too much cannabis are similar to the typical effects of using cannabis but more severe." List: extreme confusion, anxiety, paranoia, panic, fast heart rate, delusions or hallucinations, increased blood pressure, severe nausea or vomiting

claims.claim: CDC: a fatal overdose from cannabis alone is unlikely, but it is not harmless (body and FAQ)
claims.source: CDC FAQ: "While a fatal overdose caused solely by cannabis is unlikely, cannabis is not harmless."

claims.claim: A cannabis hangover can mean waking up groggy, foggy or dry-mouthed
claims.fix: now "Some people wake up still feeling a little foggy or slow, often called a cannabis hangover"; next-morning dry mouth has no source, lingering subjective effects do
claims.source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41938817/ (Matheson 2026, abstract via E-utilities): regular users tested 12-15 h after smoking had "significantly elevated VAS ratings (e.g., feeling a drug effect)"; higher-THC use linked to poorer verbal memory and processing speed

claims.claim: THC acts on cannabinoid receptors in the brain
claims.source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12648025/ (Grotenhermen 2003, E-utilities): "Cannabinoids exert many effects through activation of G-protein-coupled cannabinoid receptors in the brain and peripheral tissues."

claims.claim: NIDA: anxiety and distrust are more common with large amounts, strong products and less experience
claims.source: https://nida.nih.gov/research-topics/cannabis-marijuana (curl 2026-10-24): "These effects are more common when a person takes a large amount, the cannabis product is strong (has a high level of THC), or the person has little experience with using cannabis."

claims.claim: THC can raise heart rate right after use
claims.source: NIDA page: "Cannabis can increase heart rate and blood pressure right after use."; Grotenhermen 2003: overdosing effects include "increased heart rate"

claims.claim: Edibles are slow to start, so people often take more before the first dose lands
claims.source: NIDA page: "Edibles typically take longer to show effects. People may use more of a product as a result"; CDC FAQ: overconsumption happens with edibles "since it can take up to 2 hours to feel the effects"

claims.claim: Breathe in for four, out for six; many people find long exhales settling
claims.fix: none (framed as common experience, no health outcome claimed)
claims.source: No source needed for a breathing suggestion framed as what many people find; no medical claim is made

claims.claim: Dry mouth is common
claims.source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40268822/ (Bolt 2025, E-utilities): among 503 current users, adverse effects "included dry mouth (36.2%)", the most reported

claims.claim: CDC: alcohol and cannabis together likely cause more impairment than either alone; more impairment, more risk of harm
claims.source: CDC FAQ: "Using alcohol and cannabis at the same time is likely to result in greater impairment than when using either one alone. Greater impairment can result in greater risk of physical harm."

claims.claim: Inhaled: effects start within seconds to a few minutes, strongest at 15-30 min, taper off within 2-3 h (table, takeaway, FAQ)
claims.source: Grotenhermen 2003 abstract: "psychotropic effects start within seconds to a few minutes, reach a maximum after 15-30 minutes, and taper off within 2-3 hours"

claims.claim: Edibles and drinks: start in 30-90 min, strongest at 2-3 h, last about 4-12 h (table, takeaway, FAQ)
claims.source: Grotenhermen 2003 abstract: "Following oral ingestion, psychotropic effects set in with a delay of 30-90 minutes, reach their maximum after 2-3 hours and last for about 4-12 hours, depending on dose and specific effect."

claims.claim: The duration table comes from a widely cited review
claims.source: Europe PMC REST record for PMID 12648025 (2026-10-24): citedByCount 1011

claims.claim: Dabs follow the inhaled timeline; NIDA notes they deliver a lot of THC very quickly
claims.source: NIDA page: dabbing is "Smoking or vaporizing highly concentrated oils or extracts"; "Dabbing can rapidly deliver large amounts of THC to the body"

claims.claim: With edibles, the CDC says it may be 2 hours before you feel anything
claims.fix: now "you may not feel anything for up to 2 hours": 2 hours is the CDC's upper bound, not a typical wait
claims.source: CDC FAQ: "since it can take up to 2 hours to feel the effects from the drug"

claims.claim: CBD to counteract THC: results are mixed; a 2019 review found CBD softened some THC effects in some studies but not others (body, FAQ)
claims.source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31580839/ (Freeman 2019, E-utilities): 16 studies, 466 participants; "The findings were mixed, although CBD was found to reduce the effects of THC in several studies"; "CBD did not consistently influence the effects of THC across all studies and outcomes"

claims.claim: A 2023 randomized trial of 46 adults: CBD at common ratios did not reduce THC's effects on memory or psychotic-like symptoms (body, FAQ)
claims.source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36380220/ (Englund 2023, E-utilities): 46 healthy infrequent users, 10 mg THC with 0-30 mg CBD; recall impairment and PANSS positive symptoms "were not significantly modulated by any dose of CBD"; "At CBD:THC ratios most common in medicinal and recreational cannabis products, we found no evidence that CBD protects"

claims.claim: Black pepper: beta-caryophyllene has been studied in the lab; no human study has tested pepper for coming down from a high (body, FAQ)
claims.source: PubMed E-utilities searches 2026-10-24: (black pepper OR piper nigrum) AND (cannabis OR THC) = 10 hits, none a human test against a THC high; caryophyllene AND THC AND human terms = 16 hits, lab, rat or observational only (PMID 36648357 is an observational strain study, not a pepper test). Positive control: the matching limonene query returns PMID 38498958

claims.claim: Citrus peel has the most promising early evidence: in a small 2024 study, 20 adults who inhaled vaporized limonene with THC reported less anxiety and paranoia than with THC alone
claims.fix: now: limonene (in citrus peel) has the most promising early evidence; anxiety ratings tended to fall as limonene rose, and the only clear drop in anxiety and paranoia came at the highest limonene dose, which 12 of the 20 tried
claims.source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38498958/ (Spindle 2024, E-utilities): "Ratings of anxiety-like subjective effects qualitatively decreased as d-limonene dose increased and concurrent administration of 30mg THC+15mg d-limonene significantly reduced ratings of 'anxious/nervous' and 'paranoid'"; "a subset of participants (n=12) completed a tenth session in which 30mg THC+15mg d-limonene was administered"

claims.claim: Citrus peel contains limonene
claims.source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35413770/ (Food Chem 2022, E-utilities): "The d-limonene (DL), a bioactive ingredient in citrus peels, is a monoterpene"

claims.claim: Pine nuts: the idea points to pinene, named for pine trees; no research shows pine nuts change a high
claims.source: PubMed search pinene AND THC AND human terms = 5 hits; the one human trial, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40734690/ (Kumar 2025, N=19), found co-administered alpha-pinene "did not mitigate THC-induced memory impairment or significantly alter other acute subjective, cognitive, or physiological effects"; no study of pine nuts

claims.claim: Ginger: no study links ginger to a shorter high
claims.source: PubMed search (ginger OR zingiber) AND (cannabis intoxication OR THC) = 6 hits, none on shortening a high (chemotherapy nausea, pain supplements, chemistry, a case report)

claims.claim: None of these remedies lowers the THC in your body; time does
claims.source: Spindle 2024: d-limonene "did not alter THC pharmacokinetics"; Englund 2023: CBD had "no effect on plasma THC concentrations"

claims.claim: Give an edible a full 2 hours before more; give inhaled cannabis 15-30 minutes to peak
claims.source: CDC FAQ (up to 2 hours to feel edibles); Grotenhermen 2003 (inhaled maximum after 15-30 minutes)

claims.claim: After a break, your usual amount may feel much stronger
claims.fix: now "may feel stronger than you expect": tolerance and its reversal are documented, the size of the change is not
claims.source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30056176/ (Colizzi 2018): intoxicating effects are "blunted upon regular exposure ... (partial tolerance)"; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21747398/ (Hirvonen 2012): after ~4 weeks of abstinence "CB(1) receptor density returned to normal levels"

claims.claim: Call 911 for chest pain, fainting, trouble breathing, a seizure or someone who can't stay awake (body, takeaway, FAQ)
claims.source: CDC FAQ: "In case of emergency, call 9-1-1." (safety advice; the listed signs are standard emergencies)

claims.claim: Poison Control number is 1-800-222-1222; call it if a child eats cannabis or you're worried about too much (body, takeaway, FAQ)
claims.source: CDC FAQ: "If you or someone you know is showing signs that might suggest they have used too much cannabis, call a poison control center at: at 1-800-222-1222."

claims.claim: CDC: young children who swallow cannabis are more likely to need a hospital stay
claims.fix: precision: added the CDC's comparison, "more likely than older kids"
claims.source: CDC FAQ: "Infants or young children who unintentionally ingest cannabis are more likely to require hospital admission compared to older children who ingest similar concentrations"

claims.claim: Vomiting that won't stop can point to cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome in regular users, which NIDA says often needs medical attention
claims.fix: "In regular users" became "After long-term, heavy use", NIDA's wording
claims.source: NIDA page: CHS "is when a person has nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain after long-term, heavy cannabis use. It can recur and often requires medical attention."

claims.source: facts/hs-facts.json: "Our team is happy to guide first-time visitors and help you find products that match your preferences and comfort level." (/dispensary-locations/new-buffalo/service-areas/); About: "all of our staff is trained and knowledgeable"

claims.claim: FAQ: CBD doesn't cause a high
claims.source: CDC FAQ: "CBD is not impairing, meaning it does not cause a 'high'."

claims.claim: FAQ: children who eat cannabis can become seriously ill
claims.source: CDC FAQ: young children more likely to require hospital admission "due to their smaller size and weight and increased severity of symptoms"

claims.claim: FAQ: Poison Control can help you decide whether you need care
claims.fix: now "offers free expert advice around the clock", which is what the poison centers' own page says (poisonhelp.hrsa.gov returned 403)
claims.source: https://poisoncenters.org/ (WebFetch 2026-10-24): the Poison Help line gives "expert advice, 24/7/365 at no cost"

claims.source: Safety advice; no factual claim beyond directing readers to a vet

review.notes: Independent fact-check: CDC FAQ and NIDA topic page re-read (WebFetch, and raw HTML via curl for exact sentences); all four PubMed records re-read through NCBI E-utilities. Negative claims (no human study of black pepper, pine nuts or ginger against a THC high) were tested with PubMed searches whose positive control fired (the limonene query returns the Spindle 2024 trial); the searches surfaced a 2025 Johns Hopkins trial (PMID 40734690) in which inhaled alpha-pinene did not change THC's effects, which supports the pine-nut line, so it was left as written. Medical article: links only to blog articles and /dispensary-locations/; no shop, menu, deals or rewards link. Six sources, all opened. Writer's notes: Medical article: no shop, menu, deals or rewards links; the only store link is /dispensary-locations/ for questions in store. Black pepper, pine nuts and ginger are described as untested in people (no human studies found); the next-day paragraph is descriptive only.
